t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we study methods of isolating poisonous substances from biological fluids. Aim: to acquaint students with liquid-liquid extraction for isolating poisonous substances from blood and urine. The plan consists of two parts: liquid-liquid extraction and purification of the isolate from foreign substances. As a result, students carry out qualitative reactions, record the results in their workbook and have them confirmed by the teacher.

t: Equipment and the object of the work
n: Necessary items for the work: test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual materials. The session is held in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. Object of the work: students are given urine poisoned with phenacetin or salicylic acid.

This is the session map. The plan: liquid-liquid extraction and purification of the isolate from foreign substances. Extraction is carried out in two media: in an acidic medium with oxalic acid, and in an alkaline medium with ammonia at pH 9–10. Extraction is affected by K, R, pH, the nature of the solvent, the number of extractions, the salting-out agent and temperature. Purification methods: re-extraction, dry distillation, electrodialysis, electrophoresis and chromatography.

The general scheme of the extraction process is as follows. The pH of the urine is brought to acidic conditions with oxalic acid and shaken with 5 ml of organic solvent for 15 minutes. The aqueous layer is brought to pH 9–10 with ammonia and shaken again with 5 ml of organic solvent. Both extractions are repeated 3 times. The extracts are evaporated separately at room temperature, and the residue is dissolved in 5 ml of ethyl alcohol.

Let us memorise the key values of extraction. The volume of organic solvent is 5 ml; this is chloroform or diethyl ether. Shaking lasts 15 minutes. Each stage is repeated 3 times. At the alkaline stage the pH is 9–10. The residue is dissolved in 5 ml of ethyl alcohol. In re-extraction, pH 13 and pH 1 are used.

The first stage is acidic extraction. The pH of the urine is brought to acidic conditions with oxalic acid. Then 5 ml of organic solvent, that is, chloroform or diethyl ether, is added and shaken for 15 minutes. The organic layer is collected in a separating funnel. The process is repeated 3 times and the layers are combined.

The second stage is alkaline extraction. The remaining aqueous layer is brought to alkaline conditions, that is, pH 9–10, with ammonia. Then 5 ml of chloroform or diethyl ether is added and shaken for 15 minutes. The organic layer is collected in a separating funnel. The process is repeated 3 times.

The acidic and alkaline extracts obtained are evaporated in separate vessels at room temperature. The dry residue is dissolved in 5 ml of ethyl alcohol. Analysis for phenacetin and salicylic acid is carried out in this solution.

t: Extraction of organic acids and pH
n: The extraction of organic acids depends on pH. An organic acid dissociates in aqueous solution and is quickly hydrated by water dipoles. Owing to stable hydrate bonds it is poorly extracted. If the medium shifts to the alkaline side, dissociation increases and extraction by the organic solvent falls. If it shifts to the acidic side, undissociated molecules increase and extractability rises. Under such conditions even weak organic acids are extracted well.

t: Extraction of alkaloids and nitrogenous bases
n: Alkaloids and synthetic nitrogenous compounds form ions that dissociate with acid in a neutral medium. Undissociated organic bases are quickly solvated and pass into the organic solvent layer. Organic bases are weak electrolytes: if dissociation increases, their extraction into organic solvents decreases. Therefore, when alkali is added, extraction into organic solvents is increased. In an acidic medium, the ions remain in the aqueous layer.

The liquid alkaloids include anabasine, nicotine, pachycarpine, coniine and arecoline. In base form they are oily, volatile liquids. Their bases dissolve well in organic solvents and are distilled with steam as an azeotropic mixture. Therefore they are distilled with steam under alkaline conditions, the distillate is brought to an alkaline medium and extracted with chloroform.

Barbiturates, alkaloids and synthetic compounds are mainly crystalline drug substances and are isolated with acidified water and alcohol. According to the book, under acidic conditions, owing to the nitrogen atom in the molecule, they form salts and pass into the aqueous and alcoholic solution. Therefore, in isolating them, extraction from the aqueous solution with organic solvents is carried out.

The acidified alcohol method was proposed in 1851 by the Belgian scientist J. S. Stas for isolating alkaloids from objects of forensic chemical investigation. In 1856, F. Otto proposed purifying the alcoholic extract, and the method came to be called the Stas–Otto method. The biomaterial is infused several times with ethyl alcohol acidified with oxalic acid and left for 1 day. The alcoholic solutions are evaporated at 35 °C, 96% ethyl alcohol is added to the syrupy extract, and it is then purified 3 times with diethyl ether. Disadvantages: it takes a long time, has low sensitivity and needs costly alcohol. Advantage: isolation is possible even from a putrefied object.

Amphoteric compounds are divided into two types: those with amine and phenol groups, that is, morphine, apomorphine, salsoline, and those with amine and carboxyl groups, that is, ecgonine and amino acids. Amphoteric compounds in the molecular state are extracted well from aqueous solution by organic solvents. Their ions, however, are readily hydrated by water and are hardly extracted. At the isoelectric point they are uncharged, and proteins usually precipitate.

t: General rule: acidic and basic substances
n: We recall the general rule. Barbiturates and other acidic organic compounds are extracted well by organic solvents under acidic conditions. Alkaloids and synthetic nitrogenous compounds do not pass into the organic layer in an acidic medium but remain in the aqueous solution. To isolate them, alkali is added to the aqueous solution to convert them to the base form, and they are extracted with an organic solvent. Neutral substances such as antifebrin and phenacetin are little affected by these factors: they are extracted well under acidic, neutral and alkaline conditions.

t: Partition coefficient and degree of extraction
n: The partition coefficient K shows how completely extraction proceeds. K = Corg / Caq, where Corg and Caq are the concentrations in the organic layer and in water. The larger K is, the more of the substance passes into the organic solvent layer. R is the degree of extraction, in percent: R = A / N · 100%. Here A is the amount in the organic layer, and N is the initial total amount in water.

Complete transfer is affected by the pH of the medium, the degree of ionisation, the partition coefficient, temperature and salting-out agents. If temperature changes, the partition coefficient changes. Dissociation and association processes in the phases also change. The nature of the organic solvent also has a great effect on the degree of extraction. The salting-out agent changes the solubility of the substance.

According to the lecture, the complete transfer of a substance from the aqueous solution into the organic layer is affected by the partition coefficient and the degree of extraction. The pH conditions, the nature of the organic solvent, the number of extractions, salting-out agents, that is, electrolytes, and temperature also have an effect. Remember: the number of extractions is found experimentally.

The extracted isolate contains foreign substances such as proteins, amino acids, fat and lipids, which interfere with the analysis. Foreign substances may give the same product with reagents as the substance being tested and may adversely affect quantitative analysis. Purification methods: straining, filtration, centrifugation, precipitation and repeated extraction. Purification is based on physicochemical properties.

There are three methods of mechanical purification. Straining through cotton wool or bandage removes large mechanical inclusions, but the substance being determined may be adsorbed and lost. Filtration removes large and small inclusions, but the filter paper also adsorbs the substance and causes its loss. Centrifugation removes inclusions with an apparatus; therefore it is considered more convenient.

Proteins and interfering substances in blood are precipitated with trichloroacetic, tungstic and metaphosphoric acids and certain heteropoly compounds. Many proteins can be precipitated by heating the solution to about 40 °C. Under the action of absolute ethyl and methyl alcohol or acetone, proteins precipitate. Proteins are also precipitated by salting out with a saturated salt solution.

In purification by re-extraction, the pH of the medium must be exact. If pH is not given attention, the substance being tested may be lost. By this method, substances with neutral and weakly basic properties cannot be purified, because they are lost.

Re-extraction is carried out in two directions. For acidic substances, that is, organic acids and barbiturates, extraction is done with alkali (pH 13), then re-extraction with acid (pH 1). For basic substances, that is, alkaloids and synthetic analogues, re-extraction is done first with acid (pH 1), then with alkali (pH 13). In the basic method, weak bases are lost: purine derivatives, narcotine, promedol, antipyrine and amidopyrine.

Extraction transfers the poisonous substance from a fluid such as urine into the organic solvent layer. In extraction, acidic and alkaline media are used, shaking with 5 ml of solvent for 15 minutes, repeated 3 times. Since the isolated residue contains foreign substances, the extract is purified. There is no general exact method of purification; the method is chosen according to the physicochemical properties of the substance.

Regardless of which method is used, the chemist carries out the examination with two chloroform solutions isolated from the biomaterial. The acidic extract is tested for barbiturates, neutral substances, for example phenacetin, organic acids, for example salicylic and picric acids, and alkaloids with weakly basic properties. From the extract obtained under alkaline conditions, alkaloids and their synthetic analogues are tested. The solvent is more often chloroform.

t: The 28 substances in a full analysis
n: In a full chemical-toxicological analysis, the expert chemist must carry out testing for 28 substances of this group. They consist of 7 barbiturates, 14 alkaloids and 7 nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds. The nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds: promedol, aminazine, diprazine, tizercin, majeptil, triftazine and imizine.

t: Objects of the work: phenacetin and salicylic acid
n: We compare the two objects of the work. Phenacetin is a white crystalline powder, sparingly soluble in water and readily soluble in organic solvents. It is a neutral substance and is extracted at any pH. Salicylic acid has acidic properties. It is isolated from the object with polar solvents in an acidic medium. Neutral substances such as phenacetin are extracted well under acidic, neutral and alkaline conditions.

When electrolytes are added, the solubility of organic substances that dissolve well in water may increase or decrease. A decrease in solubility is called salting out, and an increase is called salting in, that is, enhanced dissolution. As a result of salting out, the partition coefficient increases and extraction with the organic solvent is enhanced. The salting-out effect of ions of small radius is greater than that of ions of large radius.

After isolation, the extracts from the acidic and alkaline media are in the form of residues; they contain many foreign substances. Foreign substances interfere with the analysis, may give the same product with reagents as the substance being tested and may adversely affect quantitative analysis. There is no general exact method of purification; the method is chosen according to the properties of the substance. After purification, analysis for identity and quantitative analysis are carried out.

Organic acids and barbiturates are purified by extraction and re-extraction. The residue is treated with alkali (pH 13); an alkaline aqueous layer is needed. Then re-extraction with acid (pH 1) is carried out and the substance is obtained in the organic layer. By this method, neutral and weakly basic substances cannot be purified: they are lost.

Alkaloids and their synthetic analogues are also purified by re-extraction. The residue is treated with acid (pH 1) and an acidic aqueous layer is obtained. Then re-extraction with alkali (pH 13) is carried out and the substance is obtained in the organic layer. In this, weak bases are lost: purine derivatives, narcotine, promedol, antipyrine and amidopyrine.

Dry distillation, that is, sublimation, purifies barbiturates, benzoic and salicylic acids and caffeine, which sublime on heating. Electrodialysis is used in isolating and purifying certain substances such as strychnine and pachycarpine. Alkaloid salts move through a semipermeable membrane towards the cathode under the action of direct current. For analysis, the cathode liquid is extracted.

In electrophoresis, the salts of alkaloids and basic synthetic substances move towards the cathode in direct current at different rates, and are thereby separated. In chromatography, the most widely used are thin-layer, column gel and paper chromatography. Chromatography allows not only purification from foreign substances but also determination of the identity of the substance.

t: TLC systems for purification and detection
n: We consider the systems for purification and detection by TLC. For barbiturates, the mobile phase is chloroform–n-butanol–25% NH4OH (70:40:5). For alkaloids, chloroform–acetone–diethylamine (50:30:2) or chloroform–acetone–ammonia (30:20:2). Barbiturates give an ink-coloured spot when sprayed with 0.02% diphenylcarbazone (in chloroform) and HgSO4. For alkaloids in the alkaline extract, the detecting reagent is Dragendorff's reagent.

Other purification methods are carried out together with the isolation methods. For example: filtration, precipitation of proteins with alcohol or electrolytes, and centrifugation. Precipitation of proteins helps to purify the extract from foreign substances.

t: Choosing a purification method: summary table
n: There is no general exact method of purification: the method is chosen according to the physicochemical properties of the substance. For an organic acid and a barbiturate, extraction and re-extraction are used. For an alkaloid and a synthetic base, re-extraction at pH 1 and pH 13. For a barbiturate, benzoic and salicylic acids and caffeine, dry distillation. For strychnine and pachycarpine, electrodialysis. Other purification methods are carried out together with isolation.

Review questions. What is the significance of the pH of the medium when working with aqueous solutions and organic solvents? Name and explain the methods of purifying chloroform extracts from foreign substances. Why are media of pH = 2.5–3.0 and 8.0–9.0 established? Give examples. Give examples of methods of purifying extracts from foreign substances.

We conclude. Phenacetin and salicylic acid are isolated from urine by acidic and then alkaline (pH 9–10) extraction; each is repeated 3 times. Acidic substances are extracted under acidic conditions, basic substances under alkaline conditions; pH has little effect on neutral substances. The extract is purified from foreign substances by re-extraction, sublimation, electrodialysis, electrophoresis and chromatography.
